section.title: Samson's Marriage
section.sectionRationale: The angel's promise in chapter 13 now meets the man himself, and he is not what we expected. Samson the Nazirite goes down to a Philistine town, demands a Philistine wife, kills a lion by the Spirit, hides a secret, sets a riddle, and loses both the wager and the wife. In one movement we see the deliverer's gifting and his appetites tangled together, and the startling note that the LORD is working an occasion against the Philistines through it all.
section.thesis: Samson pursues his own eyes and appetite into a forbidden marriage, yet the Spirit of the LORD rushes on him and God quietly turns even his self-willed folly into an occasion to strike the enemies of His people.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the woman at Timnah and the hidden purpose of God, verses 1 to 4; the lion torn and the honey taken, verses 5 to 9; the feast and the riddle, verses 10 to 14; the wife's tears and the secret betrayed, verses 15 to 18; and the Spirit, the slaughter, and the lost bride, verses 19 to 20.

verses.text: One day Samson went down to Timnah, where he saw a young Philistine woman.
So he returned and told his father and mother, “I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now get her for me as a wife.”

But his father and mother replied, “Can’t you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?” But Samson told his father, “Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes.”
(Now his father and mother did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an {{toanah|occasion}} to move against the Philistines; for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.)

units.label: The lion and the honey
units.note: out of the strong, something sweet

verses.text: Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother and came to the vineyards of Timnah. Suddenly a young lion came roaring at him,

and the {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat. But he did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then Samson continued on his way down and spoke to the woman, because she was pleasing to his eyes.
When Samson returned later to take her, he left the road to see the lion’s carcass, and in it was a swarm of bees, along with their honey.

So he scooped some honey into his hands and ate it as he went along. And when he returned to his father and mother, he gave some to them and they ate it. But he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s carcass.

units.label: The feast and the riddle
units.note: let me tell you a riddle

verses.text: Then his father went to visit the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, as was customary for the bridegroom.
And when the Philistines saw him, they selected thirty men to accompany him.
“Let me tell you a {{chidah|riddle}},” Samson said to them. “If you can solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.
But if you cannot solve it, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes.” “Tell us your riddle,” they replied. “Let us hear it.”
So he said to them: “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they were unable to explain the riddle.

units.label: The secret betrayed
units.note: you would not have solved my riddle

verses.text: So on the fourth day they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s household to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?”

Then Samson’s wife came to him, weeping, and said, “You hate me! You do not really love me! You have posed to my people a riddle, but have not explained it to me.” “Look,” he said, “I have not even explained it to my father or mother, so why should I explain it to you?”
She wept the whole seven days of the feast, and finally on the seventh day, because she had pressed him so much, he told her the answer. And in turn she explained the riddle to her people.

Before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city said to Samson: “What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?” So he said to them: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle!”

units.label: The Spirit and the lost bride

verses.text: Then the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty of their men, took their apparel, and gave their clothes to those who had solved the riddle. And burning with anger, Samson returned to his father’s house,
and his wife was given to one of the men who had accompanied him.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Twice in this chapter the ruach of the LORD rushes powerfully on Samson, verses 6 and 19, so that he tears the lion and strikes down thirty men. The word underlines that Samson's strength is not his own muscle but the Spirit's gift, given even to a flawed and self-willed man for the deliverance of God's people.

toanah.gloss: An occasion, opportunity, or pretext. Verse 4 reveals that the marriage Samson demands is, unknown to his parents, from the LORD, who is seeking a toanah to move against the Philistines. The word shows God working through, not around, Samson's desires, bending even a sinful choice to His purpose to break Philistine oppression.

chidah.gloss: A riddle, a puzzling saying meant to test the hearer. Samson's chidah about the lion and the honey drives the drama of the feast; it is a private secret turned into a wager, and its betrayal exposes both his cleverness and the fragility of his self-reliance, setting the pattern of secrets and betrayal that will finally undo him with Delilah.

basic.context: Samson, set apart from birth as a Nazirite to begin delivering Israel from the Philistines, goes down to the Philistine town of Timnah and demands a Philistine woman as his wife. His parents object, but he insists, because she pleases his eyes. On the way the Spirit of the LORD rushes on him and he kills a lion barehanded; later he finds honey in its carcass and eats it. At the wedding feast he sets a riddle drawn from that secret. Under threat, his bride weeps it out of him and betrays the answer to her people, and Samson, cheated of his wager, kills thirty men of Ashkelon in his rage and storms home. His wife is then given to another man. Behind it all, verse 4 tells us, God is quietly working an occasion against the Philistines.
basic.hermeneutics: This is honest history, not a model to imitate. Samson's demand for a forbidden wife, his broken secrets, his temper, and his violence are described, not commended. Yet the narrator plants a crucial clue in verse 4: this was from the LORD. God's sovereign purpose to strike the Philistines does not excuse Samson's sin, but it is woven right through it. We must hold both together: a deeply flawed man, and a faithful God working even through his folly.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on three words. Twice the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, rushes on Samson so that his strength is plainly a gift, not his own. In verse 4 God is seeking a toanah, an occasion or pretext, against the Philistines, working through Samson's very desires. And the feast revolves around a chidah, a riddle, a secret made into a wager, whose betrayal foreshadows the greater secret Delilah will later drag out of him.
basic.typology: Samson is a deliverer raised up by God, empowered by the Spirit, who strikes the enemies of God's people, and in this he faintly points to Christ. But the likeness is by contrast as much as comparison: where Samson is ruled by his eyes and his appetite, Christ is the sinless Deliverer who conquers not by grasping but by giving Himself. The lion torn open yielding sweetness hints, however faintly, at strength and death made to yield life.
basic.christ: Samson shows us how badly Israel needs a Saviour who is more than a strong man. He is a Spirit-empowered deliverer, yet enslaved to his own desires; he begins to rescue Israel while wrecking his own life. Christ is the greater Deliverer of whom Samson is only a broken shadow: also anointed by the Spirit, also raised up to save His people, but holy where Samson is self-willed, and triumphing over the true enemy by His own perfect obedience rather than his impulses.
basic.god: The startling truth of the chapter is God's sovereignty. Verse 4 tells us the marriage Samson selfishly demanded was, unknown to everyone, from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines. God does not author Samson's sin, yet He is not thwarted by it; He bends even a self-willed choice to His saving purpose. And He pours out His Spirit on an unworthy man, showing that deliverance rests on grace, not on the deliverer's goodness.
basic.crossReferences: Judges 13 gives Samson's Nazirite calling and the promise that he would begin to save Israel. Genesis 50 shows God meaning for good what men mean otherwise. Romans 8 promises that God works all things together for good for His people. And Hebrews 11 lists Samson among those commended for faith, despite his failures.
basic.oneStory: In the dark days when everyone did what was right in his own eyes, God raised a flawed Nazirite to begin Israel's rescue. Samson's forbidden marriage, his riddle, and his rage all serve, in God's hidden hand, to strike the Philistines. It is one more step in the long story of a God who saves through weak and sinful instruments, pointing forward to the sinless Deliverer who alone can truly save.

context.literary:
This begins the Samson cycle proper, the longest single account of any judge, and the last before the book collapses into chaos. The chapter is built on repeated motifs: going down, seeing, the pleasing of the eyes, the Spirit rushing, and hidden secrets. The riddle sits at its center, a puzzle the reader can solve because we alone were shown the lion and the honey, drawing us into Samson's private world and its dangers.

The chapter is framed by a striking inclusio: the Spirit of the LORD rushes on Samson at its start, verse 6, and again at its very end, verse 19, so that his worst choices, the demanded marriage, the broken secret, the wasted honeymoon, all happen inside a frame marked at both ends by the Spirit's power. The verb went down recurs three times, verses 1, 5, and 7, tracing a physical and moral descent from the hill country toward Philistine territory that mirrors the Angel's ascent in the previous chapter; where chapter 13 rose toward heaven in fire, chapter 14 descends toward compromise. The riddle scene also depends on a deliberate irony: the narrator lets the reader alone see the lion and the honey, verses 8 and 9, so that thirty Philistine guests spend three days baffled by a mystery the audience has already solved, drawing us uncomfortably close to Samson's secretive, self-reliant way of holding power.
context.historical:
Timnah was a Philistine border town in the Sorek valley, close to Samson's home region of Dan. Marriage to a Philistine violated Israel's calling to be separate, and the Philistines, a sea people with iron and five walled cities, dominated Israel at this time. A seven-day wedding feast with thirty companions and a wager of expensive linen garments reflects the customs of such celebrations.

Behind Manoah's objection lies the law's repeated warning not to intermarry with the peoples of the land, since foreign wives would turn Israelite hearts to serve other gods, Deuteronomy 7:3-4 and Exodus 34:15-16. The Philistines are not among the seven nations that law names, since they were newcomers rather than native Canaanites, but the underlying principle, that marriage bound a household to its in-laws' gods, applied with equal force to any people who did not serve the LORD, which is exactly what verse 3 means by uncircumcised, a term of covenant reproach rather than mere biology. The thirty companions supplied for the week-long feast were customary groomsmen, though a Danite strongman marrying into a Philistine border town may also have been given watchers as much as friends. Touching the lion's carcass to scoop out honey, verse 9, would have defiled a Nazirite under the law's ban on contact with a dead body, Numbers 6:6, a detail the narrator passes over without comment, letting the reader notice on his own how casually Samson was already treating a vow that was never his idea to keep.
context.canonical:
Samson belongs to the downward spiral of Judges, where even the deliverers are increasingly compromised, exposing Israel's desperate need for a righteous king and a true Saviour. His Spirit-empowerment links him to the pattern of the judges, while his moral failure looks ahead to the anarchy of the book's final chapters and, beyond that, to the coming of Christ, the Deliverer who does not fail.

The chapter also plants a phrase that will define the whole book. Samson tells his father, get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes, verse 3, and the Hebrew behind pleasing echoes the very refrain that will close Judges, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25. Samson does not merely live in an age of moral individualism, he demonstrates it in miniature, years before the narrator names it outright. His story also anticipates 1 Samuel, where another deliverer, Samuel, will finally curb the chaos this cycle produces, and where the Philistines remain Israel's chief enemy until David subdues them fully, 2 Samuel 8:1. Paul later commends Samson by name among the heroes of faith, Hebrews 11:32, a reminder that the New Testament does not erase his flaws to praise him, but praises the God who worked through a deeply flawed man, the same grace that runs through every name on that list.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To open the Samson story by showing a Spirit-gifted but self-willed deliverer, and to teach, through verse 4, that God is sovereignly working even through Samson's compromised choices to begin Israel's rescue from the Philistines.

The narrator wants his first hearers to hold two things together without collapsing either into the other: real, culpable folly in Samson, insisting on a forbidden marriage against his own parents' counsel, and real, sovereign purpose in God, who is quietly seeking an occasion against the Philistines through that very folly, verse 4. Neither cancels the other. By placing this disclosure inside a parenthesis his own parents never hear, the writer teaches his audience something about how providence actually works in ordinary life: God's larger plans are frequently invisible to the people living through them, including devout parents doing their best to counsel a wayward son. The author also intends the riddle and its betrayal to foreshadow a graver betrayal still to come, so that an alert reader already senses, watching one woman press Samson until he breaks, exactly how the story with Delilah will end two chapters later.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Samson's demands, deceptions, and violence; it does not prescribe them. His marriage to a pagan wife against his parents and his covenant, his rage, and his revenge are set before us as warnings, not examples. What endures is the truth of God's sovereign grace working through, and despite, a flawed man.

It is worth being precise about what verse 4 does and does not license. The verse explains why events happened as they did, not what Samson should have done; it is a window into God's hidden purpose, not a permission slip for defying wise counsel because something good might come of it. Believers are never told to reason from Samson's example to their own choices, marry against your parents' wisdom and trust God to use it. What is prescriptive, by contrast, is the pattern Scripture draws elsewhere from this same kind of providence: that God's people should walk in obedience and leave the larger weaving of events to Him, trusting that He can bring His purposes to pass without their needing to force outcomes through deception or self-will, as Samson repeatedly did.

debates.question: Since verse 4 says the marriage was from the LORD, is Samson excused for pursuing a Philistine wife?

views.label: God's sovereignty over Samson's sin, without excusing it
views.case: Verse 4 speaks of God's hidden purpose, not His approval. Scripture regularly shows God ordaining occasions through sinful human choices, as with Joseph's brothers, Genesis 50:20, while still holding the sinners responsible. Samson's demand remains a violation of his calling; God overrules it without endorsing it.

views.label: A providential exception in Samson's unique calling
views.case: Some argue that because God specifically raised Samson to provoke the Philistines, this particular alliance served a divinely appointed role, so the usual prohibition is, in this case, suspended by God's direct purpose.

debates.bearing: The first reading is the safer and more consistent: God's sovereignty never launders human sin. Reading it so guards us from using God's providence to excuse our own disobedience, while still assuring us that He can redeem even our failures.

debates.question: Is Samson presented as a hero of faith or as a warning?

views.label: A genuine, if deeply flawed, man of faith
views.case: Hebrews 11:32 names Samson among those commended for faith. For all his failures, his strength came by the Spirit, he acted against God's enemies, and his final prayer was answered; God truly worked through him.

views.label: Chiefly a cautionary figure
views.case: The narrative dwells relentlessly on his appetites, his broken vows, and his ruin, holding him up as a picture of Israel itself: gifted, called, yet enslaved to its own desires and sliding toward disaster.

debates.bearing: Both are true and belong together. Samson is a real instrument of God's deliverance and a sobering warning; he magnifies grace precisely because he so little deserved it, and he drives us to long for a better Deliverer.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's key words carry its meaning. Twice the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, comes powerfully on Samson, verses 6 and 19, so that the tearing of the lion and the slaughter at Ashkelon are plainly the Spirit's doing, not merely a strong man's feats; his power is gift, not achievement. Verse 4 lets us in on the secret the parents never knew: the whole marriage was from the LORD, who was seeking a toanah, an occasion or pretext, to move against the Philistines who ruled Israel. God is not reacting to Samson's choices; He is working through them, without authoring the sin in them. And the feast turns on a chidah, a riddle, born of the private secret of the lion and the honey. That secret is pried loose by tears and threats and betrayed, a small rehearsal of the great secret Delilah will one day drag from his heart.

Two more details enrich the chapter's Hebrew. When the Spirit rushes on Samson at the vineyards, the text says he tore the lion as one tears a young goat, verse 6, a small detail that becomes an unexpected echo three verses into the next chapter, when Samson takes an actual young goat to visit his wife, 15:1; the animal he once tore apart with bare hands returns as a peace offering he is not allowed to deliver. The word for riddle itself, chidah, is rare enough in the Old Testament to carry weight wherever it appears; the same word stands behind the hard questions the queen of Sheba brings to test Solomon, 1 Kings 10:1, and behind the allegory the LORD commands Ezekiel to speak over Israel, Ezekiel 17:2, so that a chidah in Hebrew is never mere entertainment but a form of testing speech, meant to expose whether the hearer has wisdom or not. Samson's riddle, framed as sport at a wedding feast, therefore carries more freight than he intends. It tests the very people who will shortly threaten to burn his bride's household to force the answer out of her, and their failure to solve it fairly, choosing coercion instead of wit, exposes exactly the kind of hearer they are. Even the phrase pleasing to my eyes in verse 3 is built on the Hebrew root for right or pleasing, the same root that supplies the book's closing refrain, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25, so Samson's very words anticipate the moral verdict Judges will finally pass on the whole era.

typology.type: Samson, the Spirit-empowered deliverer raised up to save Israel, Judges 13:25 and 14:6
typology.fulfillment: Both deliverers are anointed for their mission before undertaking it and both act under a power identified as the Spirit of the LORD, Luke 4:18, where Jesus reads Isaiah's words over Himself in the Nazareth synagogue, and Acts 10:38, where Peter says God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit and power. The correspondence ends where it matters most: Samson's Spirit-given strength operates alongside a self-willed heart that pursues forbidden marriages and revenge, while the same Spirit rests on Jesus without limit or interruption, John 3:34, so that His power and His obedience never pull in different directions.

typology.type: The riddle, out of the eater came something to eat, and the strong yielded something sweet, Judges 14:14
typology.fulfillment: Samson's private riddle describes sweetness drawn out of a dead and dangerous thing, a picture that faintly anticipates the deeper pattern of the gospel, where life is drawn out of death itself, a kernel that falls to the ground and dies before it bears fruit, John 12:24. Paul later calls the cross itself foolishness to the world and the power of God to those being saved, 1 Corinthians 1:18, sweetness the world cannot taste hidden inside what looks only like defeat. The correspondence is loose, since Samson's riddle is a private boast turned into a wager, not a proclamation, and it saves no one; the true riddle of the cross is preached openly and saves all who believe.

typology.type: God seeking an occasion against the enemy through the deliverer's own choices, Judges 14:4
typology.fulfillment: Just as the LORD works through Samson's demanded marriage without authoring its sin, He works through the very worst intentions of Christ's enemies to accomplish salvation, delivering Jesus up by His own set plan and foreknowledge even as lawless hands crucified Him, Acts 2:23. Both texts show that human freedom, even human wrongdoing, never operates outside God's sovereign plan. But the difference is total: Samson's marriage was itself a sin God overruled for good, while nothing sinful lay behind the cross on God's side, only love, so that Colossians can say Christ Himself, not merely an occasion He created, disarmed the powers and authorities there, Colossians 2:15.

study.christ:
Samson is a deliverer clothed with the Spirit, raised to rescue Israel, and in that role he points toward Christ. But he points as much by contrast as by likeness. Samson is mastered by what pleases his eyes; Christ came doing not His own will but the will of the Father, John 6:38. Samson begins Israel's rescue while ruining himself; Christ accomplishes our rescue by giving Himself. Both are anointed by the Spirit, Luke 4:18, both strike at the enemy of God's people, both bring, in a shadowy way, sweetness out of what was strong and deadly. Yet only Christ is the sinless Deliverer, and Samson's very failures make us ache for Him. Where Samson conquers in rage and appetite, Christ conquers in perfect love and obedience, and where Samson loses his bride, Christ wins His.

The temptation Samson keeps failing is named precisely by John: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life, 1 John 2:16, and this chapter is built almost entirely on the middle of those three, she was pleasing to his eyes, repeated in verses 1 and 3. Jesus meets the same category of temptation in the wilderness, when the devil shows Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory and offers them for a single act of worship, Matthew 4:8-10, and where Samson's eyes lead him toward Timnah, Christ's eyes stay fixed on the Father's will alone, refusing a shortcut to power that bypassed the cross. The contrast reaches into the wedding itself. Samson prepares a feast and demands a foreign bride against covenant wisdom, ruled by appetite; Christ, the true Bridegroom, will one day prepare a marriage supper of His own, Revelation 19:9, for a bride He wins not by taking what pleases His eyes but by giving Himself up for her, loving her into readiness rather than seizing her by force. Where Samson's wedding week ends in slaughter and a bride given to another, verse 20, the Lamb's wedding ends in a supper no one is cheated out of, and a Bride who is never given away.
study.god:
Unlike the previous chapter, God is never quoted directly here; there is no voice, no angel, no visible fire. Yet His hand is everywhere in the events themselves, the Spirit that empowers, the occasion that is sought, the timing of a lion's roar at exactly the moment Samson walks alone. This chapter therefore teaches something about God's ordinary governance that chapter 13's theophany could not: most of the time His rule over history looks like circumstance rather than speech, and the absence of visible confirmation does not mean the absence of His hand.

God's holiness and His patience sit side by side without either one softening the other. He does not strike Samson down for demanding a forbidden marriage, nor does He withdraw the Spirit that had already begun to move him in the previous chapter; the gift continues to operate through a man who is, in this very chapter, disobeying the wisdom his parents offered him. That pattern anticipates the later principle that God's gifts and His calling are not things He takes back the moment a recipient proves unworthy of them, Romans 11:29, though nothing here excuses Samson or turns the gift into an endorsement of the choice that occasioned it.

God is also, in this chapter, the God who works without needing His instruments to know they are being used. Manoah and his wife never learn what verse 4 tells the reader; they live out the story without the narrator's vantage point, exactly as most people who are swept up in God's larger purposes never receive a private explanation of how their choices are being woven into it. That should humble any reader tempted to think providence must always announce itself before it can be trusted; here it operates in full silence and is no less real for the silence, and no less gracious for going unrecognized by the very people it was quietly serving.

crossReferences.note: The law that shaped Manoah's objection warned against intermarriage with the peoples of the land precisely because foreign wives would turn Israelite hearts to other gods. Samson's parents are not being narrow when they ask about his own people, they are quoting covenant wisdom that their son overrides for the sake of what pleases his eyes.

The refrain that closes the whole book, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, is built on the same Hebrew root as Samson's own words in verse 3, she is pleasing to my eyes. Samson does not merely live through the era of the judges, his choice in this chapter is a living illustration of its final verdict.

Joseph tells his brothers that what they intended for evil, God intended for good, the same structure verse 4 applies to Samson's demand for a Philistine wife. In both stories a human choice made from selfish or even sinful motives becomes, in God's hand, the very means of saving many lives.

The Nazirite law forbade any contact with a dead body, even a close relative's, on pain of defiling the whole vow. Samson eats honey scooped from a lion's carcass without a second thought, verse 9, a small but telling sign of how lightly he was already carrying a calling he never asked to receive.

The same word rendered riddle in this chapter also describes the hard questions the queen of Sheba brings to test Solomon. A puzzle in Hebrew is a testing device as much as entertainment, which means Samson's guests are being tested by their response to it and are found wanting when they resort to threats instead of wit.

John names the desires of the eyes among the world's three besetting temptations, and this chapter runs almost entirely on that single thread, Samson pursuing what is pleasing to his eyes in both verse 1 and verse 3. The riddle and the revenge that follow are simply that first small surrender working itself out.

Where Samson's eyes are drawn toward a woman and a kingdom he was told to avoid, Jesus is shown all the kingdoms of the world and refuses them outright, worshiping God alone. The contrast measures how far a Spirit-empowered deliverer can still fall short of the obedience only Christ supplies.

Just as the LORD sought an occasion against the Philistines through Samson's own choice, so God's set plan and foreknowledge stood behind the cross even while lawless hands carried it out. Both texts insist that human agency, even at its most compromised, never operates outside God's sovereign purpose.

Paul's list of the faithful includes Samson by name alongside Gideon and Jephthah, not because their lives were exemplary but because through faith, however mixed with failure, God still worked mightily through them. The verse is a caution against reading any one chapter of a life as the whole verdict on it.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 2:24 pictures marriage as the deepest of human bonds, a man leaving his father and mother to hold fast to his wife, but by Genesis 3 desire has already begun to twist that bond into rivalry, your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you, Genesis 3:16. Samson's marriage in this chapter shows how far that twisting has traveled: a bond meant for covenant faithfulness becomes a stage for appetite, deception, and finally revenge, and the woman herself is treated first as a prize to be gotten and at the chapter's end as a possession given away to someone else, verse 20.

Yet the chapter refuses to let human folly have the last word on what history is doing. Verse 4 opens a window the rest of Scripture keeps returning to: that the LORD can use even a self-willed, appetite-driven choice as the very hinge on which His larger deliverance turns, a pattern already seen when Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good, and one that will be seen again, at infinitely greater cost, when the cross itself becomes the LORD's chief instrument for saving the world.

Israel in the days of the judges keeps repeating Eden's first mistake in miniature, trusting appetite over the wisdom God has already given, and Samson embodies that repetition personally rather than merely representing it as a national leader once did. The story therefore keeps pointing past itself. A deliverer ruled by what is pleasing to his eyes cannot be the last word for a people who need to be delivered from exactly that kind of rule, and the tension the chapter leaves unresolved, gift and folly bound together in one man, will not be untied until a greater Deliverer comes who wants nothing His Father has not given Him, and takes nothing that is not freely His to take.

quiz.q: Why did Samson insist on marrying the woman of Timnah despite his parents' objection?

options.text: Because she was pleasing to his eyes, though unknown to all it was also serving the LORD's purpose against the Philistines.
options.note: Verse 3 gives his reason, she pleased his eyes, and verse 4 reveals God's hidden purpose behind it.

options.text: Because the LORD had openly commanded him to marry her.
options.note: God was sovereignly working an occasion, but Samson acted on his own desire, not an open command.

options.text: Because his parents finally chose her for him.
options.note: The opposite: his parents objected, and he overruled them.

options.text: Because she was a faithful Israelite woman.
options.note: She was a Philistine of Timnah, which is exactly why his parents objected.

quiz.q: What was the source of Samson's strength when he tore the lion apart?

options.text: The Spirit of the LORD, who came powerfully upon him.
options.note: Verse 6 credits the Spirit of the LORD, showing his strength was a gift, not merely his own.

options.text: His years of training and unusual muscle.
options.note: He was strong, but the text pointedly attributes the feat to the Spirit rushing on him.

options.text: A weapon he happened to be carrying.
options.note: He tore the lion with his bare hands; no weapon is mentioned.

options.text: The help of his companions at the feast.
options.note: He was alone at the vineyards, and the companions came only later at the feast.

quiz.q: How was Samson's riddle finally solved?

options.text: His wife, under threat, wept the answer out of him and betrayed it to her people.
options.note: Verses 15-17 show the threat, her tears, and the betrayal of the secret.

options.text: The thirty companions were clever enough to reason it out.
options.note: They could not solve it themselves; they had to extract the answer through his wife.

options.text: Samson accidentally revealed it while boasting.
options.note: He resisted telling it; it was pried out of him by pressure, not careless boasting.

options.text: His parents told the Philistines the answer.
options.note: His parents did not even know the secret of the lion and the honey.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 tell us about God's role in these events?

options.text: God was sovereignly seeking an occasion against the Philistines, working through Samson's choices without excusing his sin.
options.note: Verse 4 reveals God's hidden purpose while Samson remains responsible for his desires.

options.text: God was surprised by Samson's actions and had to adjust His plan.
options.note: The verse shows the opposite: God was already at work through the situation, not caught off guard.

options.text: God approved of every choice Samson made.
options.note: God's sovereign purpose does not mean approval; Samson's demand still violated his calling.

options.text: God had nothing to do with these events.
options.note: Verse 4 explicitly says this was from the LORD.

quiz.q: How does Samson, the Spirit-empowered deliverer, point us to Christ?

options.text: As a flawed shadow: also anointed by the Spirit to save, but Christ is the holy Deliverer who conquers by obedience where Samson was ruled by his appetites.
options.note: Samson points to Christ by contrast as well as likeness; only Christ is the sinless Saviour.

options.text: As a perfect example whose life we should copy in every way.
options.note: Samson is Spirit-empowered, but his self-will and violence are warnings, not a pattern to copy.

options.text: As proof that strong human effort is enough to save.
options.note: His strength was the Spirit's gift, and his failures show human strength cannot save.

options.text: As a figure with no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: As a Spirit-anointed deliverer of God's people, he clearly foreshadows, however faintly, the true Deliverer.

questions: Samson was ruled by what pleased his eyes, overriding his parents and his calling. Where are your own desires quietly steering you away from what God has said?
Twice the Spirit rushed on Samson, yet his heart stayed self-willed. How do you guard against mistaking God's gifts in your life for God's approval of your choices?
Verse 4 shows God working His purpose even through Samson's compromised decision. How does it comfort you, without excusing sin, that God can weave even your failures into His good plan?
Samson kept dangerous secrets and set a riddle that would undo him. Is there a hidden area of your life that could become the crack through which you are betrayed or wrecked?
Samson's brokenness makes us long for a better Deliverer. How does seeing Christ as the sinless, self-giving Saviour, unlike Samson, move your worship this week?

translationNotes.note: This was from the LORD renders a phrase making God's hidden providence the cause behind the occasion against the Philistines; the verse does not sanction the marriage but reveals God's overruling purpose.
When the Philistines saw him carries a BSB footnote noting the sense may be when the bride's parents saw him, literally when they saw him; either way the thirty companions are provided for the feast.

On the fourth day follows the reading of the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew reads seventh, as the BSB footnote records; the fourth-day reading fits the seven-day feast and the wife's week of weeping.
If you had not plowed with my heifer is a proverbial taunt: the men only solved the riddle by working through Samson's wife, exposing the betrayal.
